tribe: Madhhij of Yemen — client of Banu Makhzum
era: The Man Whose Heart Was Weighed, Not His Tongue
teaser: They broke his tongue but not his heart. An ayah came down for him, and it is still the mercy every coerced Muslim stands on.
quran_mention: Except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith — Quran 16:106

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: Born in a borrowed house, in a borrowed city
layers.content:
His father Yasir came north out of Yemen with two brothers, looking for a fourth brother who had gone missing. The other two gave up and went home. Yasir stayed in Makka and made himself the client of a Makhzumi noble, Abu Hudhayfa ibn al-Mughira. Abu Hudhayfa married him to an enslaved woman of his household, Sumayyah bint Khayyat. She bore him Ammar, and Abu Hudhayfa freed the boy.

So Ammar grew up in a strange position: legally free, socially nothing. His people were a thousand miles away in Yemen. His protection lasted exactly as long as Abu Hudhayfa did. Ibn Sa'd notes it flatly — Yasir and Ammar remained with Abu Hudhayfa until he died, and then Allah sent Islam.

His kunya was Abu al-Yaqzan. Abdullah ibn Salama, who saw him decades later, described a tall dark man, very old. Abu Nawfal said he was one of those people who were mostly silent and had few words. His habitual phrase was a prayer: 'I seek refuge with Allah from trial.'

Ibn Sa'd's dry comment on that: then there appeared to him afterwards a great trial.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Two strangers at a door, neither willing to say why
layers.content:
He told the story himself, transmitted through his son's family. 'I met Suhayb ibn Sinan at the door of the house of al-Arqam while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was there. I asked, What do you want? He asked me, What do you want? I replied, I want to visit Muhammad and hear his words. He said, That is what I want. We went in and he offered us Islam and we became Muslim. Then we spent the day like that and left in the evening and we were concealing it.'

Ibn Sa'd places them at roughly the thirtieth and thirty-first Muslims.

What followed was not one man's decision but a household's. Yasir the father, Sumayyah the mother, Ammar, and his brother Abdullah ibn Yasir all became Muslim.

That is the detail that shaped everything after. Quraysh persecuted people according to what they could reach. A convert with a clan was insulted and threatened. A convert without one was taken out onto open ground. The family of Yasir had no clan at all — a Yemeni immigrant, a freed slave woman, and their sons. Quraysh reached all four of them at once.
layers.hadith_ref: Ammar ibn Yasir's own account, reported through Abdullah ibn Abi Ubayda — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: A hand on his head while the ground burned
layers.content:
Uthman ibn Affan remembered walking out with the Prophet ﷺ, hand in hand, across the flat ground where the family was being tortured. Yasir said only, 'Time is like that.' The Prophet ﷺ said, 'Be patient. O Allah, forgive the family of Yasir.' Yusuf al-Makki's report gives another passing: 'Good news, family of Ammar. You are promised the Garden.'

Amr ibn Maymun records what the idolaters did and what the Prophet ﷺ said over it: they burned Ammar with fire, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would pass by him and run his hand over his head, saying, 'Fire, be cool and peace for Ammar as you were for Ibrahim. The unjust party will kill you.'

A man who once saw Ammar stripped to his trousers asked about the marks on his back. 'It is from Quraysh torturing me in the hot sand of Makka.'

He emigrated to Abyssinia in the second migration, then to Madina, and fought at Badr, Uhud, the Ditch and every battle after. When the mosque of Madina was being built he carried two bricks at a time while the others carried one. The Prophet ﷺ wiped the dust off his head and said: 'Woe to you, son of Sumayya. The unjust party will kill you.'
layers.quran_ref: Quran 21:69 — «قُلْنَا يَا نَارُ كُونِي بَرْدًا وَسَلَامًا عَلَىٰ إِبْرَاهِيمَ» — 'We said: O fire, be coolness and peace for Ibrahim'
layers.hadith_ref: 'The unjust party will kill you' — narrated from Umm Salama, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Abu Qatada and Abdullah ibn Amr, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: The words they took from him, and the ayah that came back
layers.content:
There is a limit to what a body will hold, and Quraysh found his. Umar ibn al-Hakam's report says it without decoration: Ammar ibn Yasir was tortured until he did not know what he was saying.

His grandson's account gives the rest. The idolaters took him and did not let go until he had cursed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and spoken well of their gods. Then he came to the Prophet ﷺ, wrecked. 'What has happened?' 'Evil, Messenger of Allah. By Allah, I did not leave until I maligned you and spoke well of their gods.' The Prophet ﷺ asked one question, and it was not about the words. 'How do you find your heart?' 'At peace with faith.' He said: 'If they repeat it, repeat.'

Ibn Sa'd transmits through more than one chain that the ayah of compulsion was revealed about him. Abu Ubayda ibn Muhammad ibn Ammar said so; Jabir ibn Hakam said so; al-Mubarakpuri records the same, following Ibn Hisham and the commentators. The second half of the same ayah, on those whose breasts open to disbelief, was said to be about someone else.

Another report has the Prophet ﷺ finding him weeping, stroking his eyes, and telling him: they immersed you and you said such-and-such. If they do it again, say it again.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 16:106 — «إِلَّا مَنْ أُكْرِهَ وَقَلْبُهُ مُطْمَئِنٌّ بِالْإِيمَانِ» — 'except one who is compelled while his heart remains at rest in faith'
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ: 'How do you find your heart?' — reported from Abu Ubayda ibn Muhammad ibn Ammar ibn Yasir, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Persecution)

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: A governor carrying his own fodder, and a cup of milk
layers.content:
Umar made him governor of Kufa and wrote ahead: 'I have sent Ammar ibn Yasir to you as a governor and Ibn Mas'ud as a teacher... they are among the nobles of the Companions of Muhammad from the people of Badr.' Ibn Abi al-Hudhayl saw the governor buy fodder for a dirham, ask for a rope, be refused, split the load in two and carry it home on his back. When Umar later removed him and asked whether the dismissal grieved him, Ammar said that if it did, then the appointment had grieved him too.

At Yamama, part of his ear was cut away. Ibn Umar saw him standing on a stone with it hanging, shouting: 'Company of Muslims, are you fleeing from the Garden? I am Ammar ibn Yasir. Come to me.' Years later a man mocked him as maimed and he answered, 'You have insulted the better of my ears.'

At Siffin, in Safar 37 AH, an old man with a shaking spear called for a drink of milk, because the Prophet ﷺ had told him his last drink in this world would be milk. He drank it, laughed, went forward and was killed. Reports differ on his age — ninety-one, ninety-three, ninety-four.

Two men argued over who had killed him. Amr ibn al-As told them: you are only arguing about the Fire.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 29:2 — «أَحَسِبَ النَّاسُ أَن يُتْرَكُوا أَن يَقُولُوا آمَنَّا وَهُمْ لَا يُفْتَنُونَ» — 'Do people think they will be left to say We believe, and not be tested?' (Ibn Sa'd reports this was said of Ammar)
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ: 'The last drink which you drink in this world will be milk' — reported from Abu al-Bakhtari, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: When Ammar was forced under torture to say words against his faith, what did the Prophet ﷺ ask him?

options.text: 'Which words exactly did you say?'
'How do you find your heart?'
'Who forced you to say it?'
'Will you repent publicly?'

quiz.citation: Abu Ubayda ibn Muhammad ibn Ammar ibn Yasir, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ammar answered 'At peace with faith,' and was told: if they repeat it, repeat. The Prophet ﷺ did not audit the sentence. He asked after the man.

quiz.prompt: Which ayah do Ibn Sa'd's chains and al-Mubarakpuri both connect to Ammar's ordeal?

options.text: Quran 2:286 — Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity
Quran 16:106 — except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest in faith
Quran 3:139 — do not grieve, you shall be uppermost
Quran 9:40 — grieve not, Allah is with us

quiz.citation: Reported from Abu Ubayda ibn Muhammad ibn Ammar and from Jabir ibn Hakam, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; also al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: The exemption in fiqh for words spoken under coercion has a face and a name. Every Muslim since who has been forced to speak against their faith stands on the ayah that came down for Ammar.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say while passing his hand over Ammar's head as the idolaters burned him?

options.text: 'Bear it, and Badr will avenge you'
'Fire, be cool and peace for Ammar as you were for Ibrahim'
'Your reward is with Allah and needs no witness'
'Say what they want, your heart is safe'

quiz.citation: Amr ibn Maymun, reported by Yahya ibn Hammad from Abu Awana, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The wording echoes Quran 21:69, where the fire is commanded to be coolness for Ibrahim. The same report adds the warning that would follow Ammar for fifty years: the unjust party will kill you.

quiz.prompt: What did Ammar ask for at Siffin, just before he was killed?

options.text: For the banner of the Prophet ﷺ
For a drink of milk
For water from Zamzam
For his ear to be bound

quiz.citation: Abu al-Bakhtari, reported from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Prophet ﷺ had told him his last drink in this world would be milk. When they brought it he laughed, drank, and went forward. He knew what the cup meant.

quiz.prompt: How did Ammar behave when he was governor of Kufa under Umar?

options.text: He refused all salary and lived on charity
He bought fodder, was refused a rope, split the load and carried it home on his back
He built himself a fortress outside the city
He appointed his sons over the treasury

quiz.citation: Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, reported from Sufyan, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Umar's daily allowance for him was half a sheep. The witness who reports the fodder adds, almost as an afterthought, 'while he was the governor of Kufa.'

quiz.prompt: Ammar's body gave out before his heart did. Where do you think your own limit is, and how do you feel about having one?

options.text: I do not know where it is, and I would rather not find out
I have found it before, and I was ashamed
Having a limit is not a defect. It is the condition of being a body.
I trust that Allah judges the heart, so the limit frightens me less

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ammar's coercion and Quran 16:106
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Qur'an did not command him to be unbreakable. It made room for the fact that he broke, and then told him his faith was intact.

quiz.prompt: He came back to the Prophet ﷺ and confessed what he had said, rather than hiding it. What makes confession possible?

options.text: Knowing the person you tell will not use it against you
Being more afraid of carrying it silently than of saying it
Wanting a verdict, even a hard one, over uncertainty
I find it nearly impossible, and I know that costs me

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ammar's return to the Prophet ﷺ after being coerced
quiz.scholar_reflection: He arrived saying 'Evil, Messenger of Allah' before anyone accused him. The mercy in the answer was possible because he brought the wound rather than hiding it.

quiz.prompt: For decades he carried a prophecy that an unjust party would kill him, and he kept going to battle. How would knowing your ending change your living?

options.text: It would free me — the fear of death is worse than the fact
It would make me careful in a way I am not proud of
It would clarify what is worth spending days on
We all know the ending. Only the date is hidden.

quiz.citation: Reflection on the repeated prophecy transmitted about Ammar in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Others used the prophecy as a compass. Khuzayma ibn Thabit refused to fight at Siffin until Ammar fell, then said 'Misguidance is clear to me,' went forward, and was killed.

quiz.prompt: Mocked for his cut ear, he replied, 'You have insulted the better of my ears.' What is your instinct when someone points at your damage?

options.text: I hide it faster next time
I answer, and usually harder than necessary
I try to reframe it, though it does not always land
The scars I earned honestly do not sting when named

quiz.citation: Tariq ibn Shihab, reported from Qays ibn Muslim, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not deny the injury or dramatise it. He simply informed the man that he had insulted the more valuable half of Ammar's hearing.

quiz.prompt: His habitual prayer was 'I seek refuge with Allah from trial,' and a great trial came anyway. What do you make of a dua that is not answered the way it was asked?
quiz.slider_label: Trust when the dua is not granted

options.text: Refuge does not always mean avoidance — sometimes it means being carried through
He was given something better than escape: clarity about which side he was on
It troubles me, and I would rather admit that than explain it away
The dua kept him alert. A man who fears fitna recognises it when it arrives.

quiz.citation: Abu Nawfal ibn Abi Aqrab, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd sets the two facts side by side without comment: this was his constant prayer, and then a great trial appeared to him. The book leaves the tension where it is.
